lessons.title: Cost of Production and Profitability Analysis
lessons.body: To know if your cassava farm is making money, you must track every cost and every income. Start by listing all costs for one hectare. Land preparation: if you hire a tractor, it costs about $80. Cuttings: you need 10,000 stems, which cost around $50 if you buy them. Planting labour: 10 people for 2 days at $5 per day = $100. Weeding: two rounds at $60 each = $120. Fertilizer: if you use NPK, 4 bags at $30 = $120. Harvesting: 15 people for 3 days at $5 = $225. Total cost: $695 per hectare. Now, yield: a good farm produces 20 tonnes of fresh roots per hectare. If you sell at $50 per tonne, revenue is $1,000. Profit = $305 per hectare. But if you process into garri: 20 tonnes roots give about 5 tonnes garri. Selling garri at $300 per tonne gives $1,500. Subtract processing costs (grating, pressing, frying) of about $200, and you get $1,300 revenue, profit $605. That's double the profit. Always calculate your break-even point: total costs divided by price per unit. If your cost is $695 and you sell at $50 per tonne, you need 13.9 tonnes to break even. Keep records of every expense and sale in a notebook. Use a simple tool like a cash book or a mobile app like FarmDrive. This helps you know which activity is profitable and where to cut costs. Remember, family labour should be valued at market rate to see true profit. Without records, you are farming blindly.

lessons.title: Market Research and Consumer Preferences
lessons.body: Before you plant or process, find out what people want to buy. Start by visiting local markets, talking to traders, and observing what sells. In many African countries, fresh cassava roots are sold for direct consumption, but processed products like garri, fufu, and starch have higher demand in cities. For example, in Nigeria, garri is a staple; in Ghana, fufu and banku are popular. Ask questions: How much do you pay for a 50kg bag of garri? What quality do you prefer (fine or coarse)? Do you buy white or yellow garri? Note that yellow garri (with palm oil) often sells at a premium. Also, check packaging: buyers may prefer sealed plastic bags with labels for hygiene. In East Africa, cassava chips and flour are growing markets. Use simple surveys: talk to 20 potential customers. Record their answers. Look at competitor prices: if a trader sells garri at $1 per kg, you can price yours at $0.90 to attract buyers, but ensure you cover costs. Also, consider seasonality: during the lean season, prices rise. You can store garri for months if kept dry. For processed products, target institutions like schools, restaurants, and hotels. They buy in bulk and pay well if quality is consistent. A simple tool: use a notebook to track daily prices at three different markets. After one month, you'll see patterns. This research reduces risk and helps you decide whether to sell fresh roots or process. Remember, consumer preferences vary by region, so test your product in small quantities first.

lessons.title: Marketing Channels and Linkages
lessons.body: Where you sell matters as much as what you sell. Common channels for cassava products include: local village markets, urban markets, roadside stalls, supermarkets, and direct to processors. For fresh roots, the easiest is to sell to local traders who come to your farm. They pay cash but often low prices. To get better prices, form a group with other farmers and sell in bulk to urban markets. For processed products like garri, you can sell to wholesalers who transport to cities. Another channel is linking with food processing companies. For example, in Nigeria, companies like Psaltry International buy cassava for starch. They require consistent supply and quality. Contact them early and sign a contract. You can also use digital platforms: apps like AgroCenta in Ghana or Twiga Foods in Kenya connect farmers to buyers. To access these, you need a smartphone and internet. If you don't have, work through a cooperative. Also, consider adding value: package garri in branded 1kg bags and sell to supermarkets. This requires certification but gives higher margins. For linkages, attend agricultural shows and trade fairs. Network with transporters, input suppliers, and financiers. Keep a list of contacts. A simple method: create a simple flyer with your product and price, and distribute to potential buyers. Remember, reliable supply and consistent quality are key to keeping buyers. Start small, deliver on time, and grow your reputation.

lessons.title: Value Chain Financing and Credit Access
lessons.body: Cassava farming needs money for inputs, labour, and processing. Many farmers lack cash, so they need credit. Sources of credit include: microfinance banks, cooperatives, government schemes, and mobile money lenders. In Nigeria, the Central Bank's Anchor Borrowers' Programme gives loans to cassava farmers at low interest (9%). In Ghana, the Development Bank of Ghana has agricultural loans. To qualify, you usually need a group or cooperative, a farm plan, and collateral. If you don't have collateral, join a cooperative that can guarantee you. Another option is value chain financing: buyers or processors advance you inputs or cash, and you repay with produce. For example, a garri processor may give you cassava stems and fertilizer, and you pay back with roots at harvest. This is common in out-grower schemes. Also, mobile money platforms like M-Pesa in Kenya offer small loans based on your transaction history. To access, you need a registered SIM and active use. Keep records of your sales and expenses to show creditworthiness. Start with a small loan, repay on time, and build a credit history. Avoid loan sharks who charge high interest. Before taking a loan, calculate if the profit can cover repayment. For a $500 loan at 10% interest, you need to earn at least $550 extra. Use a simple budget. If you process cassava, consider leasing equipment instead of buying. Some organizations like the Cassava Adding Value for Africa (CAVA) project provide matching grants. Always read loan terms carefully. If possible, attend financial literacy training offered by NGOs. This will help you manage money and grow your business.

lessons.title: Cooperatives and Farmer Groups
lessons.body: Working alone is hard. Joining or forming a cooperative or farmer group gives you many benefits. First, you can buy inputs in bulk at lower prices. For example, a group of 20 farmers can buy fertilizer by the truckload and save 20%. Second, you can sell together to get better prices. A single farmer selling 1 tonne may get $50 per tonne, but a group selling 20 tonnes can negotiate $70 per tonne. Third, you can access credit more easily. Banks prefer lending to groups because of shared responsibility. Fourth, you can share equipment like graters and presses, reducing costs. Fifth, you can learn from each other through training and demonstrations. To form a group, start with 10-15 farmers with similar goals. Write a simple constitution: name, objectives, membership fees, and meeting schedule. Elect leaders: chairperson, secretary, treasurer. Register with the local government or cooperative department. This gives legal status. Hold regular meetings to discuss challenges and plan. Keep records of all transactions. A good example is the Cassava Growers Association of Nigeria (CGAN), which has state chapters. They help members access markets and loans. In Ghana, the Peasant Farmers Association of Ghana (PFAG) supports cassava farmers. If you join an existing group, check its track record. Avoid groups that demand high fees without benefits. As a member, participate actively. Volunteer for roles to build skills. The group can also negotiate with transporters and processors. Remember, unity brings strength. Start small, build trust, and expand. With a strong group, you can even start your own processing centre.

lessons.title: Export Opportunities and Trade Requirements
lessons.body: Exporting cassava products can bring higher income, but it requires meeting strict standards. Key export products include: cassava chips, pellets, starch, and ethanol. Major markets: China, Europe, and other African countries. For example, China imports cassava chips for animal feed and ethanol production. To export, you must first identify a buyer. Use trade portals like Alibaba or attend international trade fairs. Then, meet quality requirements. For cassava chips, moisture content must be below 14%, and foreign matter less than 2%. For starch, purity must be 99% and whiteness high. You need a certificate of origin, phytosanitary certificate, and quality analysis from a recognized lab. In Nigeria, the Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC) guides exporters. In Ghana, the Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA). You must register your business and obtain an export license. Also, consider packaging: chips are usually shipped in bulk or 50kg bags. For starch, use 25kg paper bags. Logistics: you need to arrange transport to port, customs clearance, and shipping. Costs include freight, insurance, and documentation. A 20-foot container of cassava chips (about 18 tonnes) may cost $2,000 to ship to China. Selling price may be $200 per tonne, so revenue $3,600, profit after costs. But start small: export one container to test the market. Work with an experienced exporter or agent. Also, check import tariffs in destination countries. Some countries give duty-free access to African products under AGOA or EBA. To succeed, ensure consistent supply and quality. Join an export cooperative to meet volume requirements. Keep abreast of changing regulations. Exporting is complex but rewarding if done right.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Cassava Business & Marketing Toolkit

This reference lesson consolidates the operational knowledge needed to turn cassava production into a profitable, market-driven business. It is built for African conditions â fragmented supply, thin margins, informal trade, and fast-growing urban demand for processed cassava products (gari, fufu, high-quality cassava flour, starch, ethanol). Use it alongside the other five lessons in this module as a working desk reference.

1. Cost of Production and Profitability Analysis

Cassava is often described as a "low-cost" crop, but profitability depends almost entirely on yield, labour management, and the price you capture. The single biggest cost driver is labour â planting, weeding, and harvesting can account for 60â70% of total variable costs in hand-cultivated systems. Mechanisation and improved varieties reduce unit cost per tonne.

Table 1: Indicative cost structure per hectare â cassava roots (fresh), West Africa, 2023
Cost item Share of total cost (%) Notes
Land preparation10â15Ploughing/ridging; higher with tractor hire
Planting material (stems)5â10Lower if own stems; certified TME 419 costs more
Weeding (2â3 rounds)20â30Largest labour bottleneck
Harvesting & lifting20â25Manual or semi-mechanised
Inputs (fertiliser, agrochem)5â15Often skipped, reducing yield
Transport & marketing10â15Rises sharply for distant markets

Source: FAO, "Cassava: A Guide to Production, Processing and Utilisation" (2021) and IITA Cassava Cost-of-Production studies.

Profitability formula: Gross Margin = (Yield Ã Price) â Variable Costs. At 15 t/ha and a farmgate price of US$80/t, gross revenue is US$1,200/ha; with variable costs of US$700/ha, gross margin is US$500/ha. Raising yield to 25 t/ha through improved varieties and better weed control can double that margin without expanding land.

2. Market Research and Consumer Preferences

Before planting, answer three questions: Who buys? What form do they buy? What price will they pay? Urban consumers increasingly prefer processed, packaged, and food-safe cassava products. In Nigeria, gari dominates; in Ghana, fufu and high-quality cassava flour (HQCF) for bread blending are growing; in Kenya and Tanzania, cassava crisps and starch for industrial use are emerging.

Table 2: Consumer preference signals by product and market segment
Product Primary buyers Key preference drivers
Fresh rootsRural households, local tradersPrice, freshness, low fibre
GariUrban households, institutionsGranule size, sourness, packaging
HQCFBakeries, food processorsLow moisture, <10% fibre, food safety
StarchIndustries (textile, paper, food)Purity, viscosity, consistent supply
EthanolFuel/beverage companiesVolume contracts, logistics

Source: Compiled from IITA "Cassava Value Addition" reports and African Development Bank cassava value chain studies (2022).

3. Marketing Channels and Linkages

Most smallholders sell at the farmgate to village traders, capturing the lowest share of the final consumer price. Moving up the chain â to processors, institutional buyers (schools, prisons, army), or exporters â increases margin but demands volume, consistency, and quality standards.

4. Value Chain Financing and Credit Access

Cassava has a 9â18 month growing cycle, which creates a working-capital gap. Common financing instruments include:

  • Input credit schemes â stems, fertiliser advanced against future harvest, often via cooperatives.
  • Warehouse receipt systems â use stored dried cassava or gari as collateral.
  • Value chain finance â off-takers (processors) pre-finance farmers through contracts.
  • Digital credit â mobile platforms (e.g., Tulaa, Apollo Agriculture) scoring farmers by transaction history.
  • Government & DFI windows â AfDB, NIRSAL (Nigeria), Development Bank of Ghana cassava funds.

Keep simple records (costs, yields, sales) â lenders require them. Forming or joining a cooperative dramatically improves access to credit.

5. Cooperatives and Farmer Groups

Individual smallholders rarely meet the volume, quality, or traceability requirements of processors and exporters. Cooperatives aggregate supply, negotiate better prices, share equipment (graters, presses, fryers), and access training and finance. Key success factors: transparent leadership, written by-laws, audited accounts, and a clear market contract.

6. Export Opportunities and Trade Requirements

Africa's cassava export potential lies in processed products â HQCF, starch, ethanol, chips/pellets â not fresh roots (perishable, high moisture). Key destination markets: EU (starch, ethanol), intra-African (ECOWAS, AfCFTA), Middle East and Asia (dried chips). Requirements include:

  • Phytosanitary certificate and export permit from national plant protection organisation.
  • Compliance with destination food safety standards (EU MRLs, aflatoxin limits, HACCP).
  • Consistent quality, moisture content (<12% for chips), and packaging/labelling.
  • Logistics: containerised shipping, cold chain for some products, customs documentation.
  • AfCFTA rules of origin to benefit from intra-African tariff preferences.
â  SAFETY WARNING:

Raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin and lotaustralin). Improper processing â especially insufficient soaking, fermentation, or drying of high-cyanide varieties â can cause acute cyanide poisoning (konzo, ataxic neuropathy). Always use recommended processing protocols (24â72 hours fermentation, thorough pressing and drying), prefer low-cyanide improved varieties for commercial processing, and never market inadequately processed cassava flour or gari. Train all processors on cyanide reduction and food hygiene. Store dried products in moisture-proof conditions to prevent aflatoxin growth.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Know your cost per tonne â track labour, inputs, transport; update every season.
  2. Identify your buyer before planting â fresh, gari, HQCF, starch, or export?
  3. Test yield-boosting practices â improved varieties (TME 419, TMS 30572), proper spacing, timely weeding.
  4. Add value where margin is highest â processing 1 t of roots into gari can triple revenue vs. farmgate sale.
  5. Join or form a cooperative â for volume, credit, equipment, and contract negotiation.
  6. Keep written records â required for credit, contracts, and traceability.
  7. Meet quality and safety standards â moisture, cyanide reduction, hygiene, packaging.
  8. Explore export only with a buyer and certification in place â never ship speculatively.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Cassava resources and value chain guides
  • IITA â Cassava research, varieties and agronomy
  • African Development Bank â Cassava value chain & TAAT
  • AfCFTA Secretariat â Trade rules and market access
  • FAOLEX â National food safety and export regulations database

This reference is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course "Cassava Farming and Processing," Module: Cassava Business and Marketing. Figures are indicative; always validate with local market data and extension services.

quiz.q: What is the first step in calculating profitability for a cassava farm?
quiz.explanation: You must know all costs before you can calculate profit.

quiz.q: If total cost per hectare is $700 and you sell fresh roots at $50 per tonne, how many tonnes must you sell to break even?
quiz.explanation: Break-even = total cost / price per tonne = 700/50 = 14 tonnes.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fixed cost in cassava production?
quiz.explanation: Land rent is paid regardless of production level, so it is fixed.

quiz.q: Why should family labour be valued in cost of production?
quiz.explanation: Valuing family labour shows the real economic cost of production.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for record keeping?
quiz.explanation: All can help, but a cash book is a basic record-keeping tool.

quiz.q: Which product often sells at a premium in local markets?
quiz.explanation: Yellow garri, made with palm oil, is preferred by many consumers and fetches higher prices.

quiz.q: What is a key question to ask in market research?
options: B) How much do you pay for garri?
quiz.explanation: Price is crucial for pricing your product competitively.

quiz.q: Why is packaging important for processed cassava?
options: B) It ensures hygiene and attracts buyers
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Good packaging preserves quality and appeals to customers.

quiz.q: Which institution buys cassava in bulk?
quiz.explanation: Institutions like schools, restaurants, and hotels are bulk buyers.

quiz.q: What should you do before planting a new cassava variety?
quiz.explanation: Testing preference reduces risk of unsold produce.

quiz.q: Which is a direct marketing channel for fresh cassava?
quiz.explanation: Local traders often buy directly from farms.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of selling through a cooperative?
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives can negotiate better prices due to volume.

quiz.q: Which digital platform connects farmers to buyers?
quiz.explanation: AgroCenta is an agricultural platform linking farmers and buyers.

quiz.q: What is value addition in cassava marketing?
quiz.explanation: Processing adds value and increases income.

quiz.q: Why attend agricultural trade fairs?
options: B) To network and find buyers
quiz.explanation: Trade fairs are good for building business linkages.

quiz.q: What is a common source of agricultural credit?
quiz.explanation: All these provide credit to farmers.

quiz.q: What is value chain financing?
quiz.explanation: In value chain financing, buyers or processors provide inputs or cash, repaid with produce.

quiz.q: What do you need to access a bank loan as a farmer?
quiz.explanation: Banks often require collateral, a plan, and sometimes group guarantee.

quiz.q: What is a mobile money loan platform in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: M-Pesa offers small loans based on transaction history.

quiz.q: What should you do before taking a loan?
quiz.explanation: Ensure profit can cover loan repayment.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of joining a farmer cooperative?
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives offer many benefits including bulk buying and credit.

quiz.q: How many farmers are suggested to start a cooperative?
quiz.explanation: A group of 10-15 is manageable and effective.

quiz.q: What document is needed to register a cooperative?
quiz.explanation: A constitution outlines rules and objectives.

quiz.q: Which association supports cassava farmers in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: Cassava Growers Association of Nigeria (CGAN) supports cassava farmers.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of cooperatives in marketing?
quiz.explanation: Collective bargaining gives better prices.

quiz.q: Which product is commonly exported from Africa?
quiz.explanation: Cassava chips are in high demand for animal feed and ethanol.

quiz.q: What is the maximum moisture content for export cassava chips?
quiz.explanation: Moisture must be below 14% to prevent mould.

quiz.q: Which certificate is required for exporting cassava?
quiz.explanation: All these are essential for export.

quiz.q: What is AGOA?
options: A) African Growth and Opportunity Act
quiz.explanation: AGOA provides duty-free access to US markets for African products.

quiz.q: What should a new exporter do first?
quiz.explanation: Starting small helps learn the process and reduce risk.
